Monitoring and reviewing changes to the configuration of the IaaS environment (in this case, the cloud resource hierarchy) allows for the detection and reversal of unauthorized changes to prevent exploitation.

Control AC-2 (Account Management) contains provisions for the monitoring of accounts for unusual activity and atypical usage as part of a dynamic account management approach. By monitoring these accounts, the system may be able to detect unauthorized changes to the accounts and take the necessary steps, either automatically or by alerting personnel, to remedy and mitigate the issue.

Encrypted/encoded malware is designed to hide its true purpose from an observer, meaning that signature-based methods of detection may fail. Incorporating alternative detection methods as noted in control SI-03 can provide additional avenues to detect these obfuscated malware and protect against the damage they can cause.

As polymorphic code is difficult to detect via signature-based means, non-signature-based means, pointed out in this control, should be implemented for detection. Additionally, endpoint-level fortifications should be taken to prevent the malware from inflicting damage on systems.

Enforces access control policies that restrict unauthorized queries and data retrieval from databases. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Enforces access policies that prevent unauthorized modification of domain trust objects and federation settings. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces access controls on registry keys to prevent unauthorized modification of file association handlers. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces access control policies to prevent unauthorized modification of Image File Execution Options registry keys. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforcing access control policies on Registry keys prevents unauthorized modifications to COM object references. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces access controls that prevent unauthorized users from modifying udev rule files in protected directories. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Enforces access policies on cloud management dashboards and APIs to prevent unauthorized snapshot restore or instance revert operations. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces approved authorizations to prevent unauthorized access and modifications to network device firewall rules and ACLs. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforcing information flow policies can block automated data transfers of sensitive information outside authorized channels. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least privilege restricts which users or processes can create or modify scheduled tasks and services, limiting opportunities for masquerading. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Applies least privilege to limit the permissions of accounts that can use hypervisor management tools, reducing potential impact. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Applying least privilege to container management roles and service accounts limits the permissions available to abuse CLI tools or APIs for pulling images, running containers, or executing commands. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least privilege restricts permissions on compromised accounts, reducing the ability to execute network share removal commands. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least privilege limits the permissions available to users and processes, reducing the ability to execute timestomping without elevated rights. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Applying least privilege limits the contexts and rights available for spawning processes, reducing success of PPID spoofing for privilege escalation. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits database account permissions to only necessary data and operations, reducing the scope of collectible information. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Applying least privilege to GPO permissions ensures only necessary accounts can modify them. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits privileges so only authorized accounts can add, alter, or remove domain trusts and identity provider configurations. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least privilege restricts the accounts permitted to execute esxcli commands for VIB installation or acceptance level changes. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits user and process permissions so only authorized accounts can alter system file association registry entries. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits privileges so adversaries cannot easily register traps in privileged contexts or system-wide configurations. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least privilege restricts write access to the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Netsh registry key, preventing non-administrative users from registering malicious helper DLLs. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits privileges so that only necessary accounts can modify system registry settings used for IFEO injection. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Applying least privilege ensures users lack permissions to alter COM Registry entries for hijacking. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits privileges so only necessary accounts can obtain the root access required to create or edit udev rules. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Applies least privilege to prevent non-administrative users or processes from writing to Python site-packages or dist-packages. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least privilege limits non-administrative accounts from modifying system registry locations required to abuse Active Setup for persistence. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits privileges so that only authorized accounts can invoke systemctl to execute programs as systemd services. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits permissions so that only authorized roles can execute revert or snapshot restore actions on cloud instances. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Limits privileges on network devices to only those required, reducing the ability to add, delete, or modify firewall policies. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Least privilege restricts users and processes from obtaining the administrative rights required to run netsh, PowerShell cmdlets, or registry edits that disable or alter the Windows firewall. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts remote access methods to hypervisor interfaces, limiting the ability to invoke CLIs like esxcli from external systems. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Requires authorization, monitoring, and security controls for remote access methods, directly limiting unauthorized IDE tunneling for C2. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Establishes usage restrictions, configuration requirements, and monitoring for remote access methods, directly limiting unauthorized desktop support software for C2. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Establishes and maintains baseline configurations for firmware versions on system components. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Baseline configuration establishes a known-good state without malicious Netsh helpers, enabling detection of unauthorized additions to the registry key. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Maintaining baseline configurations that specify only trusted code signing certificates limits the ability of adversaries to use stolen or unauthorized certificates successfully. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Requires documented approval and control for configuration changes such as firmware modifications. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces authorization and review for changes to configurations, blocking stealthy insertion of trap-based persistence mechanisms. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Configuration change control requires authorization and review for Registry modifications, blocking stealthy COM hijacks. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts access to make changes to system configurations including browser settings used for silent extension loading. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricting access for making configuration changes directly limits unauthorized GPO edits. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts access to configuration change functions that would allow manipulation of domain trusts or federated identity settings. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces access restrictions for changes to system components including firmware updates. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts access to modify systemd service configuration files, preventing creation or alteration of malicious services. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts access to perform configuration changes including instance reverts and snapshot restores. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces access restrictions specifically for making changes to system configurations such as security zones and ACLs. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Access restrictions for change enforce approval and control over modifications to firewall profiles, rules, and registry keys, directly limiting unauthorized alterations. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Secure configuration settings for container runtimes can disable unnecessary API exposure, enforce authentication on Docker/Kubernetes endpoints, and restrict CLI capabilities. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Secure configuration settings enforce high acceptance levels and disable force-install options to prevent malicious VIB deployment. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least functionality configuration often implements application whitelisting to block execution of unknown or unapproved binaries, directly countering padded malware. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Disabling or removing compilers and build tools from endpoints prevents compilation of delivered source code payloads. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least functionality restrictions prevent execution of unknown or non-essential binaries, reducing success of obfuscated malware regardless of junk code. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least functionality restrictions on scripting interpreters reduce the ability to dynamically execute hidden Unicode payloads. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts system functionality to essential capabilities and limits executable file types, reducing the ability to run RTLO-disguised malicious files. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Least functionality configurations restrict execution of non-essential or unapproved file types, limiting the impact of disguised malicious files. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricts non-essential system capabilities such as specific PowerShell cmdlets that enable email account enumeration. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricting the system to least functionality prevents the installation or execution of build tools like JamPlus that adversaries could abuse to run malicious scripts. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Configures systems to provide only essential capabilities, restricting or disabling browser extension installation and support. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Restricting system functionality to only essential capabilities can block or limit IDE extension installation and execution. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Configuring systems with the least functionality restricts the availability of command-line interpreters and scripting engines that adversaries rely on for executing pasted malicious code. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Configures systems to disable non-essential remote development features in IDEs, preventing their abuse for command-and-control. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces least functionality by disabling or restricting remote desktop and RMM capabilities unless explicitly required. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Configuring least functionality disables unnecessary ports and hardware interfaces that enable IP-based KVM or similar devices. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces policies governing the installation of software by users to prevent unauthorized browser extensions. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforcing policies on user-installed software directly prevents unauthorized installation of malicious IDE extensions. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Boundary protections such as firewalls and proxies can prevent unauthorized outbound automated exfiltration attempts. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Boundary protection controls, including web and email filters, prevent users from reaching malicious content that instructs them to copy and paste harmful commands. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Enforces network boundary controls to inspect, restrict, or block tunneling traffic and outbound connections used by IDE sessions. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Controls network boundaries to monitor, filter, and block traffic associated with remote desktop protocols and ports. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Boundary protection blocks access to malicious URLs or outbound connections from tools installed as a result of the attack. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Boundary protection mechanisms such as DNS proxies or gateways can filter and block resolutions to domains exhibiting fast flux patterns using threat intelligence or behavioral rules. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
Boundary protection can implement DNS filtering and egress traffic inspection to detect and block C2 channels that rely on calculated ports and IPs from DNS responses. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Employs malicious code protection mechanisms to detect and block installation of malicious browser extensions. [LLM-assisted, human QA]

Deploys malicious code protection mechanisms to detect and block malicious libraries during download, installation, or execution. [LLM-assisted, human QA]
